title: Tafkhīm & tarqīq — and the alif that has no ruling of its own
objectives: Student can define tafkhīm and tarqīq and say which ṣifah each one is the audible result of.
Student can run one heavy letter through the five levels and hear the difference between the top and the bottom of the scale.
Student can state and apply the alif rule — الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا — and produce قَالَ / كَانَ as an audibly different pair.
Student can keep the twenty-two light letters light beside a heavy neighbour, in both directions, without over-thinning them.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.6 — Tafkhīm and tarqīq, and the alif that has no ruling of its own
Same written alif, two different sounds
body: Two words. قَالَ — he said. كَانَ — he was. What is the difference?
She will say the first letter, and she is right: ق is heavy, ك is light, and she has had that since 1-14. Now the question that matters.
What about the alif in the middle? Is that the same sound in both words?

Almost every student says yes. It is written identically, it lasts the same two counts, and nobody has ever suggested otherwise. It is NOT the same sound. The alif of قَالَ is dark and back. The alif of كَانَ is bright and forward.

الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا — the alif follows what precedes it. The alif is not a heavy letter. It is not a light letter. It has no independent ruling at all, and simply extends the colour of whatever came before it.
This is the single highest-frequency error in the whole heaviness family. If only one thing survives today, make it this.

audio.cue: 10:81 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. A HEAVY alif, because ق is heavy. Dark and back, like the vowel of English 'law'.
110:3 — a LIGHT alif, because ك is light. Bright and forward. Say it straight after قَالَ, twice, exaggerated, until the difference is unmistakable.

slides.heading: Two names, and the ṣifah behind each
body: Tafkhīm (التَّفْخِيم, 'thickening') — the back of the tongue rises toward the soft palate, the mouth fills, and the letter comes out fat and rounded. The articulatory quality behind it is istiʿlāʾ, which you have had since 3-03. Istiʿlāʾ is the permanent attribute of the letter; tafkhīm is the audible result. Same thing, seen from the tongue and from the ear.
Tarqīq (التَّرْقِيق, 'thinning') — the sound comes out slim and forward, the back of the tongue stays LOW (istifāl), and the mouth does not round.
Then the sentence that makes tarqīq teachable at all: tarqīq is not a rule you apply. It is what happens when you don't do anything.
The question is never 'how do I make it light'. It is 'how do I stop leaking heaviness into it.'

Today does not teach heaviness — 1-14 taught it by ear a year ago, and 3-03 gave it its name and its count. Today turns a property into an instruction, adds the five degrees, and closes the alif gap that 1-14 left open.

slides.heading: Seven letters, and four things that switch
body: Seven letters are ALWAYS heavy — خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ, خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ. Never light, in any position, with any vowel. Everything else is light by default.
Then four standing exceptions, listed once now so you know the shape of what is coming.
ر — heavy or light depending on its vowel and the vowel before it. Lessons 3-09 and 3-10.
The ل of لفظ الجلالة — heavy after a fatḥa or a ḍamma. Lesson 3-11.
ا alif — heavy whenever the letter before it is heavy. TODAY.
The ghunnah of a concealed ن or م — heavy whenever the letter AFTER it is heavy. Unit 3.4.

Say the count out loud: two letters in the whole language switch — ر, and the ل of the Divine Name. The alif does not switch; it has no position of its own to switch from. Those two letters are the entirety of Unit 3.2, which starts in three sessions.

audio.cue: The seven from 3-03: خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ. If these are not automatic, stop and re-drill them before anything else today — everything below assumes them.

slides.heading: The performance, in three steps
body: 1. Say the letter LIGHT first — a plain English 's' — then raise the BACK of the tongue toward the roof of the mouth without moving the tip. The vowel colour darkens.
2. The mouth ROUNDS AND FILLS. Tafkhīm is felt as volume of space, not as loudness. Getting louder is not getting heavier, and you can prove it in four seconds: a quiet heavy ق, then a loud light ك.
3. DO NOT MOVE THE MAKHRAJ. The tongue tip stays exactly where the letter is articulated; only the rear rises. Sliding the tip backwards produces a different letter, not a heavier one.
That third step is the one that produces a real mispronunciation rather than a stylistic one. A ص whose tip has slid off the teeth is no longer a ص.

slides.heading: The five levels — marātib at-tafkhīm
body: Every heavy letter is heavy, but not equally. From heaviest down:
Level 1 — fatḥa FOLLOWED BY AN ALIF: غَاسِقٍ (113:3).
Level 2 — fatḥa alone: خَلَقَ (113:2).
Level 3 — ḍamma: صُدُورِ (114:5).
Level 4 — sukūn: أَعْطَيْنَٰكَ (108:1).
Level 5 — kasra: ٱلصِّرَٰطَ (1:6). Still heavy, but the lightest heavy there is.
The point is not the ordering. The point is that قِيلَ and قَالَ must not sound equally thick. Flattening the five levels into one uniform 'heavy' is the polish error at this stage.

Name the disagreement once. Ibn al-Jazarī and most later works give FIVE levels in this order. Some works give four, merging sukūn into a neighbouring level; a number of Egyptian teachers swap levels 3 and 4, putting sukūn above ḍamma. The audible difference is slight. This course teaches five, in Ibn al-Jazarī's order, and names the alternative.

audio.cue: 113:3 — LEVEL 1, the fullest heaviness in the language. A heavy letter with a fatḥa and an alif, and the alif is doing all the audible work. She memorises this ayah in four sessions.
113:2 — LEVEL 2, خ with a bare fatḥa. Two heavy letters with a light ل threaded between them.
114:5 — LEVEL 3, ص with a ḍamma. Get the ص right today. Leave the ر alone; it has its own lesson in three sessions.
108:1 — LEVEL 4, a sākin ط: heavy through the closure AND through the bounce.
1:6 — LEVEL 5, ص with a kasra. Heavy at its lightest. Do not let the kasra flatten it into a س.

slides.heading: Drill 1 — the five levels, one letter
slides.instructions: Down the scale and back up, every day. One letter, five vowels. If levels 1 and 5 sound the same, the scale has flattened and the whole set has collapsed into a switch. Run it on ق, then on ص.

audio.cue: Level 1 — fatḥa plus alif. The thickest.
Level 2 — bare fatḥa.
Level 3 — ḍamma.
Level 4 — sukūn on the ق.
Level 5 — kasra. The thinnest heavy. Say قَالَ straight after it and hear the two ends of the scale.
Level 1 on ص — fatḥa plus alif, and the alif inherits.
114:5 — level 3, ḍamma.
103:1 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Level 4, sākin ص.
1:6 — level 5, kasra. Heavy at its lightest, and it must still be heavier than a س.

slides.heading: The alif — no ruling of its own, ever
body: الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا — the alif follows what precedes it.

The alif is never listed among the heavy letters and never among the light ones. It carries no independent heaviness whatsoever. It prolongs whatever colour the preceding letter gave it, for two counts.

The reason, and it is worth saying rather than asserting: an alif has NO makhraj of contact at all. It comes from al-jawf, the empty space, shaped by nothing and stopped only by the breath running out. There is no tongue position to be high or low, so it holds the one the previous letter left behind.
Only the IMMEDIATELY preceding letter counts. In طَعَامِ the ط is two letters back and the alif is LIGHT.

Where the mistake comes from, said out loud so she stops trusting the book that gave it to her: many works state the light letters as twenty-one and list the alif among them. Where the sources disagree on the count, they agree on the practice — the alif takes the colour of what precedes it.

audio.cue: 1:7 — the alif inherits HEAVINESS from the ض. Hold the doubled ض on the side of the tongue, keep the alif dark, and only then bring the tip up for the ل.
114:1 — the alif is LIGHT, because ن is light. The cleanest light alif in her memorisation set. Contrast it directly with غَاسِقٍ.

slides.heading: Drill 2 — the alif pair
slides.instructions: The most important sixty seconds of the week. Ten alternations, every day, first. Then have someone say one at random with the board covered, and identify it by the ALIF alone — not by the first letter.

audio.cue: 10:81 — reference example. Heavy alif.
110:3 — light alif.
Reversed order, because the over-correction runs the other way. Light.
Heavy. Same written alif, four times, two colours.

slides.heading: Drill 3 — alifs in context
slides.instructions: Say which way the alif leans — heavy or light — BEFORE you read the word. Calling it first is what stops her deciding from habit.

audio.cue: 113:3 — HEAVY. The غ is heavy, so the alif is.
1:7 — HEAVY, inherited from the ض.
114:1 — LIGHT. The ن is light.
110:3 — LIGHT.
107:3 — LIGHT, and this is the item that catches her. The ط is TWO letters back. Only the immediately preceding letter counts, and that is the ع.
111:2 — LIGHT. Nothing heavy anywhere near it.

slides.heading: Contamination — the mirror error, and it arrives ten minutes later
body: Nobody heavies a ك or a ت by accident. These are the letters a heavy neighbour bleeds into: ا · ب · ل · م · ن · ه · ء.

The mechanism has a name and she should have it: INERTIA. The tongue is still up from the previous heavy letter when the light letter arrives. She is not mispronouncing the heavy letter — she is failing to switch back.
طَعَامِ (107:3) — ط heavy, then ع, ا and م all light. Most students darken all four.
ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ (1:7) — heavy غ and heavy ض with light م, و and ب threaded between them.
ٱلصِّرَٰطَ (1:6) — a light ر between two heavy letters, which is the hardest shape in the set. Do not fix the ر today. Just notice it; lesson 3-09 owns it.
And the standing rule for the whole rest of the course: EVERY ل outside the Divine Name is light, always. Say it now, because lesson 3-11 depends on it and lesson 3-12 depends on that.
Heavy fills the letter and stops at its edge.

slides.heading: Drill 4 — the drop
slides.instructions: Heavy, then immediately light, with a deliberate gap that you then close. Say the syllables apart first, then join them at speed. The drop has to be conscious before it can be automatic.

audio.cue: Broken apart. Heavy ط, then let the tongue COME DOWN before the ع. Feel the drop happen.
107:3 — joined. One heavy letter, three light ones. If the alif is dark, the tongue never came down.

grid.arabic: ٱلْـ ‑ مَـ ‑ غْـ ‑ ضُـ ‑ و ‑ بِ

audio.cue: Broken apart. Light ل, light م, heavy غ, heavy ض, then light و and light ب. Up, up, down, down.
1:7 — joined. Both degrees of heaviness in sequence with light letters threaded between them.
108:1 — a heavy sākin ط, then a LIGHT yāʾ immediately. Bounce heavy, land light.

slides.heading: Drill 5 — the reset, and Drill 6 — quiet and heavy
slides.instructions: After every round of Drill 4, one word with nothing heavy in it at all. ALWAYS end a heaviness drill on a light word — the skill is the switch, not the weight. Then four seconds on the volume confusion: قْ as quietly as you can, still heavy; كْ as loudly as you can, still light.

audio.cue: 1:2 — the reset word. Nothing heavy, nothing bounced. Three zones and no weight anywhere.
114:1 — all light, and a light alif. Leave the ر alone for now; it is heavy for its own reasons in three sessions.
106:3 — all light, and a līn yāʾ with no length.
1:7 — the all-light reset inside the hardest āyah she has. Squeezed ع, clean final ت.
As QUIETLY as you can, and keep it heavy. It is possible.
As LOUDLY as you can, and keep it light. Also possible. Therefore heavy and loud are not the same property. Four seconds, and it does not need explaining.

slides.heading: Drill 7 — every ل is light
slides.instructions: Eight words with a lām next to something heavy. Every lām stays clear and forward — the /l/ of 'leaf', never the dark /ɫ/ of 'feel'. If any of them goes velar, say the two English words out loud and try again.

audio.cue: 113:1 — two light lāms, and a heavy ق that must not reach back to either of them.
1:6 — the ل is merged here, so what you are guarding is the ص and the ط not darkening the ر between them.
97:5 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. A heavy ط with a LIGHT ل immediately after it. The hardest one in the set.
101:1 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Heavy ق, light ل, and a heavy alif after the ق.
105:2 — clamped ض, then TWO light lāms. The drag of the ض must finish before the first ل starts.
1:7 — heavy ض, heavy alif, and then a doubled ل that is LIGHT for both counts.
97:1 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Light ل before a heavy ق.
105:1 — two light lāms and nothing heavy in the word. The reset for this drill.

slides.heading: Drill 8 — level-tagging, cold
slides.instructions: Call the level NUMBER out loud before you read the word. If she reads first and labels afterwards, she is labelling the sound she just made rather than the sound the word asks for.

audio.cue: 114:5 — level 3, ḍamma.
113:2 — level 2, bare fatḥa. Twice over: خ and ق.
1:6 — level 5 on the ص, kasra.
108:1 — level 4, sukūn.
113:3 — level 1, fatḥa plus alif.
103:1 — reference example, outside your memorized surahs. Level 4, sākin ص.

slides.heading: Over-lightening — end the session here, because it is what you will hear next week
body: A student freshly drilled on tarqīq thins everything into a bright, nasal, English-sounding register — and eventually thins ص back toward س.
LIGHT IS NOT THIN. The light letters are not being done to. They are simply normal. That is the whole point of tarqīq.
Name it as a drill artefact when it appears, because it will appear within one session of the contamination fix, and a student who thinks it is a new failure loses the ground she just gained.

One honest note about the app, worth thirty seconds. Tafkhīm and tarqīq are NOT colour-coded in the mushaf highlighting she will see. The annotation dataset covers eighteen rules and heaviness is not one of them. This family has to be heard and reasoned, never looked up. That is why it gets drills and a mnemonic rather than a colour.

slides.translation: and from the evil of darkness when it settles,

audio.cue: غَاسِقٍ is the best level-1 example she has, and it is inside a surah she memorises in four sessions. غَا — a heavy letter with a fatḥa and an alif, the fullest heaviness in the language, and the alif is doing all the audible work. Contrast it directly with the alif of ٱلنَّاسِ.

slides.translation: the path of those You have blessed — not those who incurred wrath, nor those who went astray.

audio.cue: The whole lesson in one āyah. أَنْعَمْتَ is the all-light reset. ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ is both degrees of heaviness with light letters threaded between them. ٱلضَّآلِّينَ is a heavy ض with an alif that inherits from it and a doubled ل that stays light through both counts.

slides.translation: and does not urge the feeding of the poor.

audio.cue: طَعَامِ — the switch, in four letters. Heavy ط, then ع, ا and م all light. Most students darken all four. The heavy letter is correct; what fails is the switch back. Break it into syllables with a gap, then close the gap.

mistakes.wrong: A uniformly LIGHT alif — 'alif is a light letter'. قَالَ and ٱلضَّآلِّينَ read with a thin, forward alif.
mistakes.why: Many books list the alif among the twenty-one light letters, and it is the intuitive reading of 'everything outside the seven is light'. This is the flagship error of the whole family.
mistakes.fix: الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا. What came before it? Then قَالَ / كَانَ back to back, ten times.

mistakes.wrong: A uniformly HEAVY alif — the over-correction. كَانَ, مَالُهُۥ and ٱلنَّاسِ read with a dark alif.
mistakes.why: She has learned that the alif CAN be heavy and has applied it as a property rather than as an inheritance. Expect this within one session of fixing the first error.
mistakes.fix: It follows. It does not decide. Same pair, reversed order.

mistakes.wrong: Contamination from a heavy neighbour — the ع, ا and م of طَعَامِ arriving dark.
mistakes.why: Inertia. The tongue has not come down yet. She is not mispronouncing the heavy letter; she is failing to switch back.
mistakes.fix: Heavy fills the letter and stops at its edge. Drill 4 slowly, with the gap, then close it.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing heavy with loud — volume tracking heaviness across a whole line.
mistakes.why: 'Heavy' is a metaphor and loudness is the nearest available reading of it in English.
mistakes.fix: Drill 6. A quiet heavy ق, then a loud light ك. It settles the question in four seconds and does not need explaining.

mistakes.wrong: Dragging the makhraj back to 'deepen' a letter — a ص whose tip has slid off the teeth.
mistakes.why: She is trying to add depth with the only movement available to her.
mistakes.fix: The tip does not move. Only the back rises. Hold a finger where the tip should stay. This one is a real mispronunciation, not a stylistic fault.

mistakes.wrong: Flattening the five levels — قِيلَ and قَالَ equally thick.
mistakes.why: She has learned 'always heavy' and applied it as a switch. It is a scale.
mistakes.fix: Drill 1, down and back up, then ask her which end of the scale she is at.

mistakes.wrong: Over-thinning after a tarqīq drill — the whole recitation getting bright and nasal, and ص drifting toward س.
mistakes.why: Over-correction, always following a successful contamination fix.
mistakes.fix: Light is not thin. You are not doing anything to the light letters — that is the point. Name it as a drill artefact when it appears.

mistakes.wrong: The dark English 'l' everywhere — the velarised /ɫ/ of 'feel' in ٱلْحَمْدُ, ٱلْفَلَقِ and ٱلَّذِينَ.
mistakes.why: English installs it below the level of awareness, and it sounds plausible because there genuinely IS one heavy lām in the language.
mistakes.fix: 'leaf', not 'feel'. Then Drill 7, eight words, every lām clear and forward.

slides.heading: One rule, five levels, and the letter that has no ruling

audio.cue: Seven letters, always heavy, every position, every vowel. Everything else is light by default.
The alif follows what precedes it. No independent ruling, ever. Only the IMMEDIATELY preceding letter counts.
The diagnostic pair, forever. Heavy alif, light alif, same written letter. If she can do this she has the rule.
Level 1 and level 5 — the two ends of the scale. They must not sound equally thick.
107:3 — the switch. Heavy fills the letter and stops at its edge. Always end a heaviness drill on a light word.

slides.heading: Homework — 25–35 min/day, five days
tasks: One minute — Drill 2, the alif pair. قَالَ / كَانَ, ten alternations. Every day, first. Nothing else in this lesson matters as much.
Two minutes — Drill 1, the five levels, down and back up, on ق and then on ص.
Two minutes — Drill 3. Call the alif's lean BEFORE reading the word.
Three minutes — Drill 4, the drop, then Drill 5, the reset. In that order, always ending light.
Ten seconds — Drill 6. Quiet and heavy, loud and light.
Two minutes — Drill 7. Eight words, every lām clear and forward.
Two minutes — Drill 8. Call the level number before reading.
Hifz — Manzil (al-Fātiḥah), Sabqi (114:1–114:3), then new Sabaq (114:4–114:5). Twenty to forty repetitions from the page, ten extra on any corrected word.
Bring to the next session: a recording of yourself saying قَالَ and كَانَ five times each, in a random order you write down. We will see whether I can tell them apart from the alif alone.

script: Do NOT open with a definition. Open with قَالَ and كَانَ and ask what the difference is. She will say the first letter. Then ask the question that matters: what about the alif in the middle — is that the same sound in both words? Almost every student says yes.
Say them back to back, twice, exaggerated, until she hears it. Then write الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا on the board, boxed, and leave it up for the whole session.

Name the second error now, because it arrives about ten minutes after you fix the first: contamination. In طَعَامِ the ط is heavy and the ع, the alif and the م are light. Most students darken all four. The heavy letter is correct; what fails is the switch back.

Say explicitly what today is and is not. 1-14 taught her heaviness by ear, and taught it the right way round — you hear the dome on the VOWEL beside the letter, not on the consonant. 3-03 gave her خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ, the count of seven and twenty-two, and the two degrees. Today turns that property into an instruction, adds the five degrees, and closes the alif gap.
Check the seven letters in the first two minutes. If خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ is not automatic, stop and re-drill it — everything today assumes it.

Connect each name to its ṣifah and say the framing sentence verbatim: tarqīq is not a rule you apply, it is what happens when you don't do anything. The question is never 'how do I make it light' but 'how do I stop leaking heaviness into it.'

List the four standing exceptions once and then defer them, so she knows the shape of what is coming: ر (3-09, 3-10), the ل of the Divine Name (3-11), the alif (today), the ghunnah of a concealed ن/م (Unit 3.4). Then say the count: two letters in the whole language switch.

Teach the performance in three steps and make her do each separately. The third is the one that matters most — the tip does not move, only the back rises. Sliding the tip back produces a different letter, not a heavier one.

Teach the five levels as ONE letter run through five vowels: قَالَ · قَدْ · قُلْ · يَقْطَعُ · قِيلَ. Down and back up. The point is not the ordering; it is that قِيلَ and قَالَ must not sound equally thick.

Name the disagreement once, as the methodology requires. Ibn al-Jazarī and most later works give five levels in this order; some give four; a number of Egyptian teachers swap levels 3 and 4. This course teaches five in Ibn al-Jazarī's order and names the alternative.

Give the alif its OWN block of the session. Do not fold it into the levels. It is never listed among the heavy letters and never among the light ones, because it has no makhraj of contact at all — it comes from al-jawf and has no tongue position to be high or low.
Drill the diagnostic pair until she can identify one by the alif alone with the board covered. Then do it in her own memorisation set: غَاسِقٍ heavy, ٱلضَّآلِّينَ heavy, ٱلنَّاسِ light.
Tell her where the mistake comes from: many books state the light letters as 21 and list the alif among them. Where the sources disagree on the count, they agree on the practice.

Name the letters that need vigilance — ا ب ل م ن ه ء — and give the mechanism its name: inertia. Then drill heavy → light transitions slowly, with a deliberate gap, until the drop is conscious. ALWAYS end a heaviness drill on a light word.

Say the standing rule she needs for the rest of the course: every ل outside the Divine Name is light, always. صَلَاة and طَلَبَ have heavy neighbours and light lāms. Lessons 3-11 and 3-12 both rest on this.

ٱلصِّرَٰطَ has now appeared in three consecutive lessons and it will appear in three more. Today it is level 5 — heavy under a kasra — and it contains a light ر between two heavy letters. Do NOT fix the ر today. Notice it and move on; 3-09 owns it.

قَالَ is the only example here from outside al-Fātiḥah and the last ten surahs. It is worth the exception because no clean level-1 minimal partner for كَانَ exists inside her range. Label it out loud: reference example, outside your memorized surahs.

End the session on the mirror error, because it is what you will hear next week. Over-lightening: everything thins into a bright, nasal register and ص drifts toward س. Light is not thin. Name it as a drill artefact when it appears.

Thirty seconds on the app, honestly. Tafkhīm and tarqīq are not colour-coded; the dataset covers eighteen rules and heaviness is not one of them. This family has to be heard and reasoned, not looked up.

Hifz: Manzil (al-Fātiḥah) and Sabqi (114:1–114:3) first, then new Sabaq 114:4–114:5. Today's rule fires in both new āyāt, so use them — صُدُورِ is level 3 (get the ص right, leave the ر alone), and ٱلْوَسْوَاسِ and ٱلْخَنَّاسِ are almost entirely light, with the cleanest light alifs in her whole memorisation set. Use them as the reset against صُدُورِ.

listenFor.item: The alif of قَالَ dark and the alif of كَانَ bright — the same written letter carrying two colours.
listenFor.commonMistake: A uniformly light alif. قَالَ, طَابَ and ٱلضَّآلِّينَ read with a thin, forward alif. This is the flagship error of the whole family.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Many books list the alif among the twenty-one light letters, and it is the intuitive reading of 'everything except the seven is light'.
listenFor.correctionCue: الْأَلِفُ تَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهَا. What came before it? Then قَالَ / كَانَ back to back, ten alternations.

listenFor.item: A light alif after a light letter, even in the week after the alif rule has landed.
listenFor.commonMistake: A uniformly heavy alif — كَانَ, مَالُهُۥ and ٱلنَّاسِ read dark. Expect it within one session of fixing the first error.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has learned that the alif can be heavy and has applied it as a property rather than as an inheritance.
listenFor.correctionCue: It follows. It does not decide. Same pair, reversed order.

listenFor.item: The tongue coming DOWN at the edge of a heavy letter — طَعَامِ with three genuinely light letters after the ط.
listenFor.makhraj: The back of the tongue, which must return to istifāl before the next letter begins. The tip is not involved.
listenFor.commonMistake: The ع, ا and م of طَعَامِ arriving dark; the ل of any word with a heavy letter in it going velar.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Inertia. The tongue has not come down yet. She is not mispronouncing the heavy letter — she is failing to switch back.
listenFor.correctionCue: Heavy fills the letter and stops at its edge. Drill 4 slowly, with the gap, then close it.

listenFor.item: Heaviness independent of volume — a quiet ق that is still heavy.
listenFor.commonMistake: Volume tracking heaviness across a whole line.
listenFor.whyItHappens: 'Heavy' is a metaphor and loudness is the nearest available reading of it in English.
listenFor.correctionCue: Drill 6. Quiet and heavy, loud and light. Four seconds, and it does not need explaining.

listenFor.item: The makhraj held still while the back of the tongue rises.
listenFor.makhraj: For ص, the tip stays between the incisors at tongue point 9. Only the rear rises toward the soft palate.
listenFor.commonMistake: A ص whose tip has slid off the teeth, giving something between ص and a retroflex.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She is trying to add depth with the only movement available to her.
listenFor.correctionCue: The tip does not move. Only the back rises. Hold a finger where the tip should stay.

listenFor.item: Five audibly different degrees of heaviness on one letter.
listenFor.commonMistake: قِيلَ and قَالَ equally thick — the scale flattened into a switch.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has learned 'always heavy' and applied it as an on/off property.
listenFor.correctionCue: Drill 1, down and back up, then ask her which end of the scale she is at.

listenFor.item: Light letters that are simply normal, not thinned.
listenFor.commonMistake: The whole recitation getting bright and nasal after a tarqīq drill, with ص drifting toward س.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Over-correction, and it always follows a successful contamination fix rather than preceding it.
listenFor.correctionCue: Light is not thin. You are not doing anything to the light letters — that is the point.

listenFor.item: Every lām clear and forward — the /l/ of 'leaf'.
listenFor.makhraj: Tongue point 5 — the tongue's edge from rear to tip at the gums of the upper front teeth, with the back of the tongue LOW.
listenFor.commonMistake: The velarised /ɫ/ of 'feel' in ٱلْحَمْدُ, ٱلْفَلَقِ and ٱلَّذِينَ.
listenFor.whyItHappens: English installs it below the level of awareness, and it sounds plausible because there genuinely is one heavy lām in the language.

teacherNotes.homework: 25–35 min/day over five days. Daily, in this order: Drill 2, the alif pair قَالَ / كَانَ, ten alternations (one minute — first, every day, and nothing else in this lesson matters as much); Drill 1, the five levels down and back up on ق then ص (two minutes); Drill 3, calling the alif's lean before reading (two minutes); Drill 4 the drop then Drill 5 the reset, in that order, always ending light (three minutes); Drill 6, quiet and heavy, loud and light (ten seconds); Drill 7, eight lāms all clear and forward (two minutes); Drill 8, calling the level number before reading (two minutes). Hifz: Manzil (al-Fātiḥah), Sabqi (114:1–114:3), then new Sabaq 114:4–114:5, twenty to forty repetitions from the page with ten extra on any corrected word. Bring to the next session: a recording of قَالَ and كَانَ said five times each in a random order written down, so we can see whether the two are tellable apart from the alif alone.
